clauses.text: The official documents (the Brumaire decree and the Year VIII Constitution) establish the change of authority through formal legal mechanisms: the creation of a provisional consular commission (A0017) and the appointment of three consuls for ten years (A0002).

evidence.exact_text: The Corps-Legislatif creates provisionally a consular executive commission, consisting of Citizens Sieyes, Roger-Ducos, and General Bonaparte, who shall bear the name of Consuls of the French Republic.
The government is confided to three Consuls appointed for ten years and indefinitely re-eligible.

clauses.text: Bourrienne's memoir states that Bonaparte's remarks at St. Cloud were confused and devoid of dignity and sense (A0010, A0012), contradicting any later narratives claiming a coherent speech.

evidence.exact_text:
All the speeches which have been subsequently passed off as having been
delivered by Bonaparte on this occasion differ from each other; as well
they may, for he delivered none to the Ancients, unless his confused
conversation with the President, which was alike devoid of dignity and
sense, is to be called a speech.

There was not the slightest
connection in what he stammered out. Bonaparte was then no orator. It
may well be supposed that he was more accustomed to the din of war than
to the discussions of the tribunes.

clauses.text: The memoir emphasizes the contingent nature of the coup, suggesting that failure and even Bonaparte's execution were real possibilities (A0009, A0013).

evidence.exact_text:
Who could tell which of the two things
would happen!  Success legalised a bold enterprise, which the slightest
accident might have changed into a crime.

Instead of
sleeping next day at the Luxembourg he would, I am convinced, have ended
his career on the Place de la Revolution.

clauses.text: Bourrienne's memoir characterizes Bonaparte's St. Cloud remarks as confused and undignified, while the official proclamation and decree present the coup as a necessary response to a failed constitution and corrupt Directory, creating a tension between the personal, contingent account and the official narrative of necessity.
